steps.body:
"Significant" answers exactly one question: **could chance alone have done this?**

It does not answer:

– Is the effect **big**?
– Does it **matter**?
– Is it **true**?

With a large enough sample, an effect of 0.3 points on a 100-point test becomes significant. It is real, and it is worthless.

explanationVariants: A huge sample shrinks the wobble, so even a 0.3-point gap sits far outside what chance produces. Significance says the gap is real; it says nothing about the gap being useful.
Effect size is a separate question, answered in the units of the problem: 0.3 points on a 100-point test.

widget.prompt: An app is tested on 100,000 students and raises scores by 0.3 points on a 100-point test, with p < 0.001. Should the school buy it?

options.label: Probably not — the effect is real but far too small to be worth the cost.
options.feedback: Right. The p-value certifies that 0.3 is not a fluke. It has no opinion on whether 0.3 is worth paying for.

options.label: Yes — p < 0.001 is very strong evidence.
options.feedback: Strong evidence for a tiny effect is still evidence for a tiny effect. Strength of evidence and size of effect are separate axes.

options.label: Yes — with 100,000 students, the effect must be large.
options.feedback: Backwards. A large sample lets you DETECT tiny effects, so a huge n and a tiny effect are a natural pairing.

options.label: No — with p < 0.001, the result is too good to be true.
options.feedback: A small p-value is not suspicious in itself, and with n = 100,000 it is exactly what you would expect even from a trivial effect.

explanationVariants: Significance and effect size vary independently: a big effect can be non-significant in a small study, and a tiny effect can be significant in a huge one.
Always read both: is it real (p), and is it big enough to act on (effect size)?

widget.prompt: Which of these findings is worth acting on?

items.label: +12 points, p = 0.002, n = 800
items.feedback: Big effect, and chance struggles to explain it. Both questions answered well.

items.label: +0.2 points, p = 0.001, n = 200,000
items.feedback: Real, and pointless. The enormous sample detected an effect too small to change any decision.

items.label: +11 points, p = 0.30, n = 12
items.feedback: Promising size, but twelve students cannot rule out luck. This is a reason to run a bigger study, not to act.

items.label: +9 points, p = 0.01, n = 500
items.feedback: A useful size with evidence behind it — the pairing you actually want.

widget.missFeedback: Check both axes: is chance ruled out (p), and is the effect big enough to matter (size)?
widget.successFeedback: Real and big is the only combination worth acting on. Real and tiny, or big and unproven, are both reasons to wait.

widget.prompt: Draw from 50,000 users at increasing sample sizes. Watch what happens to a difference that is real but tiny as the sample grows.
widget.successFeedback: As n rises the wobble shrinks, so a smaller and smaller true difference stops being explainable by chance. That is all 'significant' means. A 0.3-point gain on a 100-point test is significant at n = 100,000 and still worthless — significance is about chance, never about size.
widget.methodFeedback: A biased method produces a difference that is not real at all, which significance testing cannot detect. Fix the design before asking about p.
widget.sizeFeedback: Push the size higher. The effect being demonstrated only becomes visible once the wobble is small enough to make a tiny gap stand out.
widget.drawsFeedback: Repeat the draw — the claim is about how the SPREAD of estimates behaves as n grows, which needs more than one.

steps.body:
Three more things a significant result does not give you:

**Proof.** About 1 significant result in 20 is a fluke when nothing is going on.
**Generalisation.** It applies to the population you sampled, not to everyone.
**Cause** — unless the treatment was randomly assigned. Significance and causation are different questions with different guardians.

explanationVariants: Random assignment buys causation. A small p-value buys only 'chance alone is a poor explanation of this gap'.
Significance in an observational study means the association is unlikely to be a fluke — the lurking variable is still standing there untouched.

widget.prompt: An observational study finds coffee drinkers sleep 40 minutes less, p < 0.001. What follows?

options.label: The association is unlikely to be a fluke — but coffee causing it is still unproven.
options.feedback: Right. The p-value defends against chance; only random assignment defends against lurking variables. Two different guards, two different gates.

options.label: Coffee causes people to sleep less.
options.feedback: Nobody flipped a coin here: the drinkers chose coffee themselves. People who already sleep badly may reach for coffee, so the arrow can run the other way entirely.

options.label: Nothing, because observational studies mean nothing.
options.feedback: That overcorrects. The study establishes a real association, which is genuinely useful — it just cannot be promoted to a cause.

options.label: The result would be causal if the sample were larger.
options.feedback: Sample size never converts an association into a cause. Only the design can do that.

hints: Check the design first: was anything randomly assigned? Then check the effect size, in its real units.
It is an observational study, so 'cuts risk' is a causal claim the design cannot carry.
And the effect is 0.4 percentage points — real, perhaps, but tiny. Both problems must appear in the honest version.
explanationVariants: The honest version keeps the association, drops the causal verb, and states the effect in its actual units: people who ate the food had a 0.4-point lower rate, and the study cannot say the food did it.
Two separate overreaches: 'cuts' asserts cause from an observational design, and the headline hides how small 0.4 percentage points is.

widget.prompt: "Eating kale cuts heart-disease risk (p < 0.001)" — from an observational study where kale-eaters had a 0.4-percentage-point lower rate. Which rewrite is honest?

options.label: "Kale-eaters had a 0.4-point lower rate — a small, reliable association, not evidence that kale is the cause."
options.feedback: Right — it fixes both overreaches: the causal verb and the hidden effect size.

options.label: "Kale is strongly linked to heart health (p < 0.001)."
options.feedback: "Strongly" describes the evidence against chance, and readers will hear it as the size of the effect. The effect is 0.4 points, which is not strong at all.

options.label: "Kale may cut heart-disease risk slightly."
options.feedback: Better on size, but "may cut" still smuggles in the causal claim that an observational design cannot support.

options.label: "There is no evidence kale affects heart disease."
options.feedback: That throws away a real finding. There IS an association, well-supported against chance — it simply is not a cause, and it is small.

steps.body: Significant answers one question and stays silent on the rest.
takeaways: Significance rules out chance. It says nothing about the SIZE of the effect — and a huge sample makes trivial effects significant.
It is not proof (about 1 in 20 clears the bar by luck) and it does not generalise beyond the population sampled.
It never buys causation. Only random assignment does that.
steps.teaser: Last chapter: take these tools into the wild and judge real claims.

concept.body: Ask two questions of every finding, never one. **Is it real?** — that is the p-value's job. **Is it big?** — that is the effect size's job, measured in the units of the problem. A yes to the first and a no to the second means: real, and not worth doing.

explanationVariants: p < 0.001 answers 'is it real'. Nothing here answers 'is it big enough to matter'.
The size of the effect must be reported in real units — minutes, points, dollars — or the finding cannot be acted on.

widget.prompt: A study reports only: "the effect was statistically significant (p < 0.001)". What is missing?

options.label: The size of the effect.
options.feedback: Right. Without it you know chance is a poor explanation, but not whether the finding is worth a penny.

options.label: Nothing — p < 0.001 says it all.
options.feedback: It says only that chance is unlikely to have produced the gap. A gap of 0.1 points can clear that bar with a big enough sample.
